Quoted-placeholder anti-pattern: three CHECK_RUNNERS wrap a template interpolation in literal single quotes, which defeats postgres.js parameter binding and indicates the author believed these were string-pasting interpolations. packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:222 is `sql`created_at ${postgresOperators(operator)} '${date}'`` with `date = param1_9.date` read from the attacker-supplied params at line 221; lines 202 and 211 are `sql`${sql(field + "_text")}::text ${operator} '${regexPattern}'`` and `sql`${sql(field + "_text")} ${operator} '${regexPattern}'``. The graph records a FLOWS_TO self-loop at line 222 (src==dst), marking the argument as already tainted by untrusted input. Separately and visible in the same code, line 217 `sql`length(${sql(field + "_text")} ${postgresOperators(operator)} ${length}`` has an unbalanced opening parenthesis after `length(` with no closing paren, so the `length` filter emits syntactically invalid SQL. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the verifier: the resolved version is NOT present in this graph — the Dependency node set contains only 5 entries, all root-level dev tooling, so the backend's package.json was not captured. The verifier must read packages/backend/package.json (and any lockfile) to pin the installed koa-router version and check it against advisories before this is reported as a known-vulnerable component; the grounded claim here is the unscoped/abandoned package choice and its blast radius, not a specific CVE.

leads.text: An overly-permissive email-validation regex literal `/^\\S+@\\S+$/` is duplicated across all four authentication/registration forms, accepting malformed addresses. The identical literal appears in packages/frontend/pages/login.tsx:33, packages/frontend/pages/signup.tsx:68, packages/frontend/pages/join.tsx:95 and packages/frontend/pages/request-password-reset.tsx:26, each as `email: (val) => (/^\\S+@\\S+$/.test(val) ? null : "Invalid email")` inside a Mantine `useForm` validate block. `\\S+@\\S+` requires only one `@` with any non-whitespace on both sides, so it admits values with no TLD (`a@b`), no dot, multiple `@` (`a@b@c`), and embedded quotes/angle-brackets/control characters — anything without whitespace. Two concerns: (1) this is client-side-only validation in the browser bundle and is trivially bypassed regardless, so any server-side consumer that trusts the format is exposed — relevant because these same addresses flow into the invite/verification email paths; (2) the pattern has two adjacent greedy `\\S+` quantifiers around a single literal, giving polynomial (not exponential) backtracking on long non-matching all-non-whitespace input. Shape D: the defect is the literal's permissiveness, not the `.test()` call. Lower severity than the other leads — recorded for completeness since Shape D covers pattern-in-literal defects.
